title: Multi-armed bandits: final test
note: Goal G only (how greedy, ε-greedy and UCB choose). Every item is parallel to a practice principle but uses a setting the practice doesn't (banner ads, office coffee machines, a study app, podcasts), so the test measures transfer, not recall of practice items. type: base = recognise the idea; apply = pick and justify in a given state; transfer = a new situation.

items.prompt: An online shop shows each visitor one of five banner ads and wants as many clicks as possible. Seen as a multi-armed bandit, what are the options you choose between (the “arms”)?
options: The visitors
The five banners
The clicks
The days the shop is open
items.explain: The arms are what you choose between in every round. Each visitor is a round, and a click is the reward.

items.prompt: Why can't the shop simply pick the best banner on its first day?
options: Because the shop is only allowed to change banners once a week
Because all banners have the same click rate at first
Because each banner's true click rate is unknown, and single visitors click more or less at random, so the shop has to learn the rates by showing the banners
Because the best banner changes every day
items.explain: The averages are hidden and each reward is random, so the only way to learn how good a banner is, is to show it and average the results.

items.prompt: Your office has three coffee machines. So far you rated the coffee from machine A 7 and 5, from B 8, and from C 6, 6 and 7. Following greedy, which machine do you use next, and why?
options: B, because its average so far (8) is the highest
A, because its best cup (7) is as good as C's
C, because it has the most ratings and is the most reliable
Any of them, chosen at random
items.explain: The averages are A = 6, B = 8, C ≈ 6.3. Greedy always picks the best average so far, even if it rests on a single cup.

items.prompt: A study app uses greedy to choose between two lesson formats. Format A is truly better (70% of students pass, against 55% for B). The first student who got A happened to fail; the first who got B passed. What does the app do from then on?
options: It soon switches to A, because A is better on average
It alternates between A and B to be fair
It picks A or B at random for every student
It keeps using B: after one try A's pass rate looks like 0%, and greedy never tries A again to find out
items.explain: Greedy only uses the option with the best average so far. One unlucky first result can hide the better option for good, because greedy never tries it again.

items.prompt: The shop switches to ε-greedy with ε = 0.1 for its five banners. When it explores, it shows one of the five at random. What share of visitors see the banner with the best average so far?
items.explain: 90% of visitors get the favourite on exploit visits, and 1 in 5 of the remaining 10% get it by chance: 0.9 + 0.1/5 = 0.92.

items.prompt: Which statement describes how ε-greedy explores?
options: It always explores the option it has tried least
It explores less and less as its averages become reliable
On a fixed share of rounds it picks any option at random, even ones it already knows are bad
It explores only until it has found the best option, then stops
items.explain: With probability ε it picks at random, ignoring what it knows. That share stays the same however long it runs, so known-bad options keep getting picked.

items.prompt: A friend tries one dish at a new restaurant, likes it, and orders exactly that dish on every visit from then on. What does this strategy risk?
options: Missing a better dish, because other dishes are never tried
Wasting many meals on dishes already known to be worse
Nothing: one visit tells you how good a dish really is
Spending too much, because favourites are expensive
items.explain: Only exploiting means never exploring: a dish that wasn't tried (or was unlucky once) never gets another chance, so a better one can stay hidden. Too much exploring would be the opposite risk.

items.prompt: A podcast app recommends shows with UCB. Show A has an average rating of 4.1 from 500 listeners; show B has 3.9 from 4 listeners. Why might UCB recommend B next?
options: Because UCB picks at random on some rounds
Because B has the higher average
Because UCB always recommends the newest show
Because B's average comes from very few listeners, so B gets a large bonus, and its average plus bonus can beat A's
items.explain: An average from 4 listeners is much less reliable than one from 500. UCB adds a bonus that is bigger for options tried less, giving B the benefit of the doubt.

items.prompt: Under UCB right now, option A has average 6.0 and bonus 0.3, B has average 5.2 and bonus 1.2, and C has average 5.8 and bonus 0.4. Which option does UCB pick?
options: A
B
C
One of them at random
items.explain: Scores: A = 6.3, B = 6.4, C = 6.2. UCB picks the highest average plus bonus: B, although A has the best average.

items.prompt: UCB keeps picking option B, which turns out to be only average. What happens?
options: B's bonus grows with every pick, so UCB sticks with B
B's bonus stays the same, so UCB picks B forever
B's bonus shrinks with every pick; once its average plus bonus falls below another option's score, UCB moves on
UCB switches to a random option after a fixed number of picks
items.explain: Each pick makes B's average more reliable, so its bonus shrinks. If B isn't really the best, its score drops below another option's and UCB moves on, without any random picks.
